body: I believe that always comparing the CTEs (simple `==` should suffice) would also work if the CTEs aren't cloned.

the `==` operator is overloaded in SQLAlchemy, we have an expensive system to compare statements however SQLAlchemy uses object identity to indicate the uniqueness of a construct as rendered in a SQL statement, ~~so "statement comparison" does not generally apply to the complication phase~~ (edit: it is actually falling back on that here).  for the issue at hand, you can't have two CTEs with the same name so the error is correct, the issue is that the aliased() construct is somehow causing the single CTE to be split into two, and I would assume the two CTEs have a common parent so maybe the check here needs to consider that topology
oh wow that codepath is actually using compare(), OK.   havent seen this in awhile, but yes that needs to be using compare
oh one of them is the annotated form, that's all.   OK this is something simpler then

this reproduces, so not within ORM

```
# fails
a = select(A).where(A.i > A.j).cte("filtered_a")._annotate({"foo": "bar"})
ac = a.c

```

this issue has a simple workaround which is to use the CTE directly without using aliased() (see test case at the top).  There's no compelling reason for the CTE to be inside of aliased() since it's not the row returning construct in the query.  if you have some structure where you are receiving an existing `aliased()` you can access the CTE like this

```
a = aliased(A, select(A).where(A.i > A.j).cte("filtered_a"))

# this is the CTE on the inside
a = inspect(a).selectable

```

`a = inspect(a).selectable` is a nice touch.
I got a strange issue where when not using the hack I get multiple unrelated CTE error while the version with the hack results in recursion. The patch helps.
